#501. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship."

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions."

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax

The team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

The addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

The pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an important maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

The new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

The findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical."

#500. Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

Colorful metaphors, a near-miss with Eddie Murphy and humpback whales in 20th-century California.

It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales".

After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp?

Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.

They gave him freedom to tell the story he wanted to tell, and he landed on a not obviously box-office-friendly formula of "No dying, no fighting, no shooting, no photon torpedoes, no phaser blasts, no stereotypical bad guy". It was a massive shift away from Khan and Kruge, the grandstanding villains in movies II and III.

Nimoy also wanted the film to have an environmental message and appeal beyond the franchise's traditional fanbase. The film would actually be promoted with minimal "Trek" branding in some territories.

"I wanted to make it accessible to people who don't go to 'Star Trek' movies," Nimoy said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman. "I wanted to make it a movie-movie. It starts out like a 'Star Trek' movie and then makes a left turn. It is intentionally very different."

"The Voyage Home" effectively closes the trilogy that began four years earlier with "The Wrath of Khan". The story picks up three months after Spock's regenerated body is reunited with his katra (spirit), though nobody ever explains why Kirk and the rest of the crew are all still wearing exactly the same clothes. Following the self-destruction of Enterprise over the Genesis Planet, the gang are heading back to Earth to face the music for a lengthy rap sheet that includes grand theft starship and insubordination on an epic scale.

But as they voyage home (geddit?) in a reconditioned Klingon Bird-of-Prey nicknamed the Bounty — complete with a cloaking device that will come in very handy when hiding in Golden Gate Park — they learn that an alien probe of unknown origin (one of the coolest "Star Trek" spaceships) is tearing Earth apart looking for humpback whales. With the species extinct since the 21st century, the crew travel back in time via one of the most surreal sequences in "Star Trek" history — Morphing CG heads? What the hell was Nimoy thinking? — in the hope of finding the whales that might just be able to ask politely if the probe might leave us alone.

Screenwriters Steve Meerson and Peter Krikes were assigned to the project early on (working with Nimoy and producer Harve Bennett on the story), and their treatments included a future Earth under threat from a plague and a discarded subplot about Lt. Saavik being pregnant with Spock's child as a result of the pon farr mating ritual. There were also discussions about the Bird-of-Prey decloaking above the Super Bowl, and — most bizarrely of all — a guest-starring role for Eddie Murphy as an astrophysicist who wants to believe in aliens.

Murphy was both a Trekkie and one of the biggest stars on the planet at the time but ultimately decided to make notorious stinker "The Golden Child" instead. "In retrospect, I think I might have been better off doing 'Star Trek IV'," he said later. Paramount had also gotten cold feet about putting the star of the highly lucrative "Beverly Hills Cop" in its highest-profile franchise.

"Paramount said, 'We're not going to put out [our] two most valuable assets in one movie – so start over, folks!'" said Nicholas Meyer (h/t The Telegraph), hired to retool the script after Murphy's departure. "That's why I was called at the last minute."

Meyer was already "Star Trek" royalty, having brought the movie series to life as director and uncredited writer of "The Wrath of Khan". Indeed, he's arguably the reason the "odd numbers bad/even numbers good" theory of "Trek" films persisted for so long, having later gone on to co-write and direct "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country".

He shared scripting duties with Bennett, with the producer writing the 23rd-century-set bookends of the film, and Meyer handling everything in present-day California. Weirdly, Meyer had prior experience bringing a time traveler to contemporary San Francisco in his 1979 HG Wells/Jack the Ripper adventure "Time After Time".

With the three previous "Star Trek" movies largely studio-based, "The Voyage Home" marked a rare chance for cast and crew to head out on location. The Monterey Bay Aquarium filled in for the Cetacean Institute (slightly implausible home of humpbacks George and Gracie), while the USS Ranger — moored in San Diego and no stranger to Hollywood after "Top Gun" — guest-starred as a nuclear "wessel".

Kirk and co. also headed out onto the streets of San Francisco. Nimoy had toyed with giving them '80s-appropriate disguises, but changed his mind when he realized nobody would bat an eyelid at their 23rd-century civilian attire.

Aside from some second unit work photographing humpbacks off the coast of Hawaii, the whales themselves were mostly animatronics created by Industrial Light & Magic. "One of the reasons we think that ['The Voyage Home'] really didn't win visual-effects awards is people didn't really understand how good [the whales were]," said executive producer Ralph Winter. "ILM did such a good job on those whales that they went on tour for a year or more around the world to museums because the expertise, the art, and science of what they had done was very good."

Meyer, meanwhile, fully embraced the opportunity to write a fish-out-of-water comedy, with this seasoned crew of Starfleet veterans struggling to get their heads around the eccentricities of late 20th-century America.

Kirk and Spock experiment extensively with "colorful metaphors" — "double dumbass on you!" — while Kirk gets out of paying for dinner by using the convenient excuse that money isn't a thing in the future. Scotty (James Doohan) attempts to talk to a mid-'80s Apple Macintosh via a mouse before he risks screwing with the timeline by 'inventing' transparent aluminum decades early.

And in the film's most famous moment, Spock delivers a Vulcan neck pinch to a punk playing his music very loudly on a public bus, winning extensive applause from his fellow passengers in the process. The nuisance rocker was played by Nimoy's assistant, Kirk Thatcher, who co-wrote the "I Hate You" song that plays on that era-authentic ghetto blaster. He later returned to the role in "Star Trek: Picard", though this time he responded more apologetically to Seven of Nine's request to turn it down.

Kirk is undoubtedly the center of the movie, pulling the strings and getting his first romantic interest since the Original Series — whale expert Dr Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks), who eventually accompanies the Enterprisers back to the future. But "The Voyage Home" also gives the supporting bridge crew — all of whom reveal a talent for comedy — more satisfying character beats than they'd ever had before. Walter Koenig's W-heavy pronunciation of "vessels" would later be adopted by Anton Yelchin when he inherited the role in JJ Abrams' "Star Trek".

The crew eventually makes it out of the 20th century alive, with the whales safely secured in a giant fish tank so they can make contact with the probe. Of course, what George and Gracie actually say when they arrive in the future remains a mystery; despite Bennett's insistence that the whale song conversation should be subtitled, he was wisely overruled by Nimoy.

With Earth saved from death by giant cigar, the Enterprise crew have all their charges revoked, bar one, as Kirk is 'busted' down to Captain. The crew is then gifted the shiny new USS Enterprise-A, freeing them to continue exploring the cosmos on the big screen.

Which they did, with Shatner taking advantage of a so-called "favored nations" clause in his contract — which meant Paramount had to match anything offered to Nimoy — to direct the rather less positively received "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier", before Meyer returned for "The Undiscovered Country".

Nimoy delivered on his promise to appeal beyond the traditional fanbase, and his reward for earning "Star Trek"'s biggest ever box office haul — a record "The Voyage Home" would hold until Abrams went Trekkin' in 2009 — was directing smash-hit comedy "Three Men and a Baby" the following year. The film also paved the way for "The Next Generation", as Paramount realized the franchise's massive potential, but decided they wanted to cash in without paying mega-bucks for the legacy cast.

Hardcore fans will often claim they prefer the more serious themes of "The Wrath of Khan", "First Contact" or even "The Motion Picture" to "The Voyage Home", but "Star Trek" has rarely been as joyous or fun as on this madcap jaunt to the 20th century. "The One with the Whales" really is one for the ages.

'Star Trek: The Voyage Home' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

#498. NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman

An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find new planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (#17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov

Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

Hubble's most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.

NASA's Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will settle essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#497. What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.

Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.

The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory

Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.

Astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.

The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.

One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.

A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.

Marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.

This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.

What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks

The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.

Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.

This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.

Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.

The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.

Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.

However, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.

While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.

Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

Materials provided by The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#495. Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

Physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

The achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out."

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty big loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer."

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

He also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

The dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

"If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse said. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion."

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

The physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse said. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time."

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

Using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

In earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

The team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

"Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse said. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century."

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).

#494. Eye of the Sahara

The Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

#493. A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system. Images captured between September 16 and 24, 2026, revealed a previously unknown comet, the first discovered by the mission.

The achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets. The speed with which researchers identified and confirmed the discovery demonstrates that Euclid can detect new comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun. This capability could eventually help identify a target for ESA's upcoming Comet Interceptor mission.

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium. Pöntinen developed specialized software to detect and track small solar system objects appearing in the telescope's images.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images -- the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas."

The object appeared in a region of the sky known as the 'Euclid Deep Field North'. Over several days, the telescope captured it in five separate fields of view, taking between two and four exposures of each field for a total of 16 exposures.

After searching catalogs of known asteroids and comets without finding a match, Pöntinen submitted the observations to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a potential new comet. The report enabled astronomers using telescopes on Earth to carry out additional observations. On October 8, the MPC officially confirmed the discovery. The comet has been designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The newly discovered comet is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth. That distance is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point somewhere between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

However, the comet is traveling well outside the relatively flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun. It is currently positioned almost directly above the Sun, following a sweeping path over the solar system that will take thousands of years to complete.

The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) serves as the central international hub for observations of asteroids and comets. It gathers data from observers around the world to verify discoveries, determine orbital paths, and assign official designations. As additional observations become available, astronomers will be able to calculate the orbital period of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) more precisely.

Although Euclid has spotted comets before, all of them had already been discovered. Several aspects of the telescope's design and observing strategy make finding previously unknown objects within our solar system especially difficult.

Euclid intentionally avoids the region of the sky surrounding the plane of the solar system, where large numbers of asteroids and comets can be found. Dust concentrated in this region produces unwanted light that could interfere with the telescope's sensitive observations of the distant universe.

The spacecraft also follows a 'step-and-stare' observing strategy, typically imaging each section of the sky only once. This means researchers cannot readily direct Euclid back toward a newly detected comet to gather more information about it.

Identifying objects within our solar system is nevertheless an important part of Euclid's scientific work. Researchers must account for everything appearing in its images so that unrelated features, including comet trails and unwanted light, can be removed without compromising the accuracy of its galaxy measurements.

"Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet's orbit and Euclid's scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images," says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, and part of the discovery team.

Euclid's unexpected discovery also provides valuable experience for scientists working on ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission. Although the newly identified comet is not an appropriate destination for the spacecraft, the successful detection and rapid notification process demonstrates how the two missions could work together to identify potential targets.

"While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on," adds Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

Comets are ancient bodies composed of ice and dust that remain from the formation of our solar system approximately 4.6 billion years ago. Most originate in the distant Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, regions located beyond the orbits of the outer planets (interstellar comets come from other solar systems).

As a comet approaches the Sun, increasing temperatures cause its ice to turn directly into gas. Escaping gas and dust form a glowing, fuzzy cloud known as a 'coma,' as well as an extended tail.

Because comets native to our solar system have remained relatively unchanged since their formation, they preserve valuable evidence of the materials and environmental conditions that existed when the planets were taking shape. Studying these ancient objects may also help scientists understand the origins of Earth's water and the chemical building blocks of life.

Euclid's Hunt for Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The primary goal of the Euclid mission is to uncover how dark matter and dark energy influence the visible universe. During its six-year survey, the space telescope will examine the shapes and movements of billions of galaxies at distances reaching up to 10 billion light-years.

The comet discovery was reported on behalf of the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium by M. Pöntinen, A. A. Nucita, A. Franco, M. Granvik, B. Altieri, S. Kruk, B. Y. Irureta-Goyena and B. Carry.

#492. Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

“Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” said Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

“The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” said Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

“We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she said. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she said. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#490. German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

Two German film students confronted the American who won festival prizes with their animated movie. "The Talented Mr. F," their documentary on their fight against plagiarism, is now in the spotlight.

It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."

What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

#489. Investigators make progress in hunt for cause of FAA ground stop

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Investigators said within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

#487. NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can quickly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#486. Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago.

Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams”.

In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago.

To an untrained eye the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world.

Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground. Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood, partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface.

Our new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet.

Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions.

But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few meters) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models.

These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor.

They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water.

To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques.

First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves.

Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside.

The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes.

This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface.

The results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It shows that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think.

Understanding where voids may exist underground can be important for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works, mitigating geological hazards, and accessing and protecting groundwater resources.

Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and supply water to 10–25% of the global population.

More fundamentally, caves are important scientific archives. Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time.

Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have evolved and adapted in isolation. These are some of the least studied organisms on Earth.

To learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard.

The implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide promising exploration sites for life on other planets.

Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves, including some thought to be related to karst on Mars.

The Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be attractive bases for future human explorers.

How many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too.

Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand.

The authors would like to acknowledge Matthias Leopold from The University of Western Australia; Rok Ciglič, Mateja Ferk, Jure Tičar, Matija Zorn and Matej Jelovčan from the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts (ZRC SAZU); John A. Webb from La Trobe University; Uroš Stepišnik, Matej Dolenec, Primož Miklavc, Tomislav Popit and Andrej Šmuc from the University of Ljubljana; and Jian-xin Zhao from The University of Queensland.

#484. How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble

From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."

To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."
