#483. Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

"Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond."

Brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.

"We were very lucky," said Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project."

Hidden records of ancient tsunamis and earthquakes

Beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

Earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have important implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The study, titled "Discovery of the deep-sea NEOM Brine Pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea," was published on June 27, 2022, in Communications Earth & Environment.

The research team included Sam J. Purkis, Hannah Shernisky, Peter K. Swart, Arash Sharifi, Amanda Oehlert, Gaëlle Duchâtellier, James Klaus, Gregor P. Eberli, Larry Peterson, and Graham Kolodziej from the UM Rosenstiel School; Fabio Marchese and Francesca Benzoni from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Red Sea Research Center; Giovanni Chimienti from the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy; Andrew Craig and Mattie Rodrigue from OceanX; Jürgen Titschack from MARUM -- Center for Marine Environmental Sciences in Germany; and Ameer Abdulla from NEOM.

NEOM, a company developing the Saudi Arabian coastline, provided funding for the four-week research expedition aboard the OceanXplorer.

The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

#481. NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement

How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

#477. Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island

New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”

So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

#476. The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

Men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but new research has uncovered one striking difference. In an experiment designed to recreate the demands of everyday life, men ignored conversational questions more than twice as often as women while performing just as well on the other tasks.

Whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them. Although women are widely believed to be better at multitasking than men, previous research has found only minor and inconsistent differences between the sexes, raising doubts about the accuracy of this popular assumption.

With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.

In their study, "Men Talk Less Than Women During Multitasking," published in the scientific journal Psychological Research, the researchers developed an experiment involving five different activities. The setup was designed to capture the complexity of everyday multitasking more accurately than most previous studies.

The first experiment involved 41 men and 37 women. Participants were asked to follow a recipe in a kitchen setting, look up phone numbers, match numbers with letters, watch a slideshow for specific words, and answer conversational questions. A new question was posed every 20 seconds (e.g., "Would you rather lose all of your money and valuables or all of the pictures you have ever taken, and why?").

In a second experiment, the researchers recruited 160 observers to determine whether differences in multitasking behavior were noticeable to others. Without being given prior information about the participants or findings, the observers watched video recordings of the experiments and assessed how well the participants performed.

One Surprising Difference Between Men and Women

Men and women achieved comparable results on four of the five activities. Conversation, however, revealed a notable exception. Men left conversational questions unanswered more than twice as often as women. When men did answer, their responses were just as fast and of comparable quality to those given by women.

The researchers suggest that women may, on average, be more inclined to engage in communication during social interactions. However, the study did not directly investigate this possibility, so the explanation should be treated with caution. The results are also consistent with evolutionary theories suggesting that women may have a greater tendency to engage in conversation.

How Conversation Shapes Perceptions of Ability

The differences in conversational engagement appeared to have a considerable impact on how others judged the participants. Observers rated men as having less control over the activities, performing more poorly, putting in less effort, and being less alert than women. They also perceived men as less happy and as deriving less enjoyment from the experience.

Rather than revealing a broad difference in multitasking ability between men and women, the research points to a much more specific behavioral distinction: men are more likely to leave conversations unanswered when managing several activities simultaneously.

Because conversational engagement is easily noticed by others, this difference may create the impression that men are less effective at multitasking, even when their performance on other activities is comparable to that of women. The findings offer a potential explanation for how the popular stereotype that women are better multitaskers developed and why it continues to persist.

"Taken together, our data confirm that there are no substantial sex differences in cognitive visual-manual tasks, but that significant sex differences do exist in the ability to hold a conversation while multitasking," explains André Szameitat. This is "an ability highly salient in everyday life and, thus, could explain the development of the widespread public stereotype that women are better at multitasking than men," the researcher concludes.

#474. Bombed factories, billion-dollar opportunity: Why German companies are staying in Ukraine

German companies remain committed to Ukraine despite million-dollar losses, an unreliable energy supply and a shortage of skilled workers. They are betting on new markets and long-term growth.

Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses and residential buildings: The massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under fire, affecting German companies.

"Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs said. "We are preparing for a difficult winter."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks."

Energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

"Not a single German company has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine and the software in Germany.

A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," he said.

For foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act. On the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following 10 years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin.

"German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted. However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks."

Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he added.

At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment."

Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: Companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the company and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different. When investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.

#471. This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal. New research published in Nature is challenging its long-established place in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility.

The 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae. Nicknamed "Lizzie" because of its resemblance to a lizard, the specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved in two crushed slabs of rock. Early descriptions relied largely on anatomical features visible at the surface, including four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These characteristics distinguished Westlothiana from many other animals living at the time, whose limbs more closely resembled fins.

Although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land. Amniotes are a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Following its scientific description in 1990, Westlothiana became an important reference point for researchers investigating when and how these animals first evolved.

"Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades," said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. "But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected."

Advanced X-Ray Scans Reveal Lizzie's True Identity

Using powerful X-ray imaging technology at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, the scientists peered beneath the surface of the rock and reconstructed previously inaccessible parts of the animal's anatomy.

What they discovered was strikingly different from the anatomy expected in an early reptile. Lizzie possessed a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a mouth resembling that of a fish, complete with thousands of tiny teeth. Together, these features rule out its previously proposed position within the evolutionary lineage leading to reptiles. Instead of living primarily on land, Westlothiana appears to have been an aquatic or amphibious animal.

"The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought," said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford.

Reptile-Like Features Evolved in Aquatic Ancestors

The discovery also changes how scientists understand the origins of several anatomical features traditionally associated with vertebrates adapted to terrestrial environments.

Researchers now believe that characteristics such as claws and the arrangement of five digits on each hand and foot, a pattern familiar in reptiles and mammals, had already emerged in earlier animals that were still closely associated with water. These creatures belonged to the evolutionary lineage leading to tetrapods, the broader group of four-limbed vertebrates that encompasses both amphibians and amniotes.

"This is a big surprise," said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum's Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. "It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more 'primitive' than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles."

Ancient Footprints May Tell a Different Story

The findings could also have important implications for the interpretation of prehistoric fossil tracks. Recently discovered trackways have been used as evidence that amniotes first appeared during the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago.

These ancient impressions record the movements of a four-limbed animal with apparently clawed digits. However, if distant relatives of tetrapods such as Westlothiana also possessed claws, such footprints are no longer sufficient on their own to identify the animals that left them as amniotes.

Some trackways previously attributed to early amniotes may instead have been left by more ancient, amphibious creatures belonging to the evolutionary lineage of tetrapods.

"The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water," Jenkins said.

Additional contributors to the study include Jason Head from the University of Cambridge, Vincent Fernandez from the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Lucy Roberts from the Natural History Museum, London, and Timothy Smithson from the University Museum of Zoology Cambridge.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (grant number EAR-PF 2518154), the National Environment Research Council (grant numbers NE/S000739/1, NE/W007576/1, and NE/L002507/1), and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (grant number BB/X014819/1).

#469. Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress

Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."

Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `

The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

#465. CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed runners-up.

Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."

"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

#462. A24 is having a great year at the box office. That could give HBO Max a streaming edge

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The company plans to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

Paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The company has said it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

#459. Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.”

Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him.

“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security.

Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”

While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs.

“The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang said. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.”

The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”

Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in.

“It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human,” he said. “And this company has been more than gracious, more than thoughtful, more than fair in giving me a second chance.”

Huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct.

Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his self-described “deeply intense, insanely intense” management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far.

“It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there.

“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide.

Huang acknowledged during the meeting that Trump was a vocal supporter of Nvidia but insisted that politics played no role in how the company operated. “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said. “He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president.”

Huang said he would take the same approach with future US presidents. “We are the most apolitical company,” he said. “I don’t love that we talk about politics here. I love that we talk about work here.”

Huang also sought to reassure women at Nvidia, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women” and touting the company’s flexible work policies, which he said allow employees to simultaneously build their families and careers.

“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” Huang said.

After Huang’s resignation, he and the company’s board received criticism from Wall Street for not having an obvious internal successor in line. Huang addressed the issue head-on during the company meeting. “I don't believe in succession planning; I think it’s flawed,” he said, specifying that the concept may make sense but the implementation often causes issues.

Huang described each of his 60 reports as CEOs of their own units who could step up when he eventually leaves. “It creates resilience, and it creates the opportunity, which is ultimately the responsibility of the board, to give them the opportunity to decide at that time what the world needed, what the company needed, and be able to choose from a large collection of amazing people,” he said.

The CEO also argued that his brief absence had demonstrated Nvidia’s ability to operate without him. “I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.

#456. Black Friday scams: How to protect yourself as cyberattacks threaten retailers

With Black Friday almost upon us, it's time to talk about something other than what you should buy or how much it costs.

The biggest shopping day of the year in the United States can also be one of the most precarious, thanks to an increased reliance on e-commerce in the age of rampant cyberattacks and system outages. There's only so much that you, as an individual shopper, can do to protect yourself if an online retailer is compromised or if you're targeted by a scam artist, but it's important to understand those measures regardless.

Here are some common-sense things you can do to make sure Black Friday doesn't become a massive headache for you or your family.

One of the main ways that bad actors will try to get you during this holiday shopping season is through phishing, which describes a variety of techniques used by scammers to trick people into giving up money or personal information.

For example, you may get text messages or emails warning of an urgent problem, such as someone using your card to buy something fraudulently, or something more mundane like a delivery notification. While you don't want to outright ignore these warnings because there is always a slim possibility that they are real, you need to double and triple-check things like the sender's email address or a URL or phone number they've given you to solve the "problem." Email phishing requests tend to come from odd-looking, non-standard email addresses, or ones that are misspelled in some way. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Generally speaking, companies will not reach out to you over text or email urgently asking for payment or personal information. If you encounter something like this, you can quickly run a Google search of the number, address, or the nature of the request, and you'll potentially find other people warning against the phishing scam. Above all else, exercise as much caution as possible and, if needed, reach out directly to the company in question if you need to verify a request of some sort.

Retailer websites usually give users the ability to make an account or otherwise save payment and shipping information to make the checkout process more straightforward. You can do this if you want, but given the number of cyberattacks against retailers, doing so puts your information at risk of being compromised.

There is no perfect solution because no form of online payment is 100 percent free from danger. However, using services like Apple Pay or even PayPal can allay the risk a little bit, especially if you use secure multi-factor authentication for those services. In fact, you should use MFA and strong, unique passwords for every account you need to have. It's even better to use a good password manager, which can come up with strong passwords for you that you don't even need to remember.

Lastly, sometimes around Black Friday, you'll see deals that seem incredibly generous. Maybe an 80-inch OLED TV is going for $150, or a TikTok account is promising the Nintendo Switch 2 for under $100. In these cases, it's best to understand that you might be getting taken for a ride. Black Friday deals aren't that good, unfortunately.

Sadly, there's no hard-and-fast rule to follow here, other than "be wary of anything that seems too good to be true." That's especially true if the deal is coming from a website or service you've never heard of before. It's one thing to see screaming good deals on slightly more trustworthy platforms like Amazon, but another thing entirely if the retailer in question is obscure or sketchy.

#455. iRestore Elite Laser Hair Growth System Review: Husband-Approved

The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.

I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.

However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.

Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.

Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.

Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)

The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.

The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.

If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.

The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.

During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.

Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.

The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.

Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.

In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.

The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.

The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)

Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.

As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

#454. EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?

Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

#451. Why is everyone saying ahh almost almost? The viral Twitch meme, explained.

Monkey D. Luffy is once again at the scene of the internet's latest viral meme. Well, technically, it's Twitch streamer Jynxzi playing as the beloved One Piece protagonist in Fortnite, but the distinction hardly matters when you're watching the aspiring King of the Pirates repeatedly fail to obtain a pirate token.

Sometimes, the funniest thing you can do on the internet is fail spectacularly. Or, in Jynxzi's case, come agonizingly close to succeeding.

If you've spent any time scrolling through TikTok or Instagram Reels lately, you've probably heard his now-viral refrain: "Ahh, almost, almost." What began as a moment of frustration on Twitch has since become the internet's go-to response to everything from missed basketball shots to the everyday indignities of being alive.

Here's what you need to know about the "ahh almost almost" meme and how it escaped the confines of Twitch.

The voice behind the meme belongs to Jynxzi, a popular Twitch streamer known for his animated reactions and exaggerated competitive spirit. With 11.8 million followers on Twitch, Jynxzi regularly streams games like Rainbow Six Siege, League of Legends, and Fortnite, often collaborating with other streamers like iShowSpeed and StableRonaldo.

The meme appears to have originated from a Fortnite livestream in early November, during which Jynxzi repeatedly tried (and failed) to obtain an in-game pirate token. Adding to the comedic effect was his declaration that he was putting in the work while everyone else was out partying. Despite his apparent dedication, success continued to elude him.

Clips of the stream began circulating on TikTok in early November, and it didn't take long for the audio to take on a life of its own outside of the gaming community.

At its most basic, the meme is a reaction to a near miss. But part of what makes it so funny is the gap between how much confidence and effort someone brings to a task and how little they have to show for it. Sometimes, the person in question isn't even remotely close to succeeding, which makes Jynxzi's insistence that he's "almost" there all the more amusing.

One popular iteration of the trend pokes fun at hustle culture. Videos begin with someone ostensibly working toward a goal, accompanied by the caption "while they're out partying btw," before cutting to footage of them failing at the very thing they've been practicing.

On TikTok, students document their study sessions only to reveal their failing test grades, a skier attempts a jump and loses their skis in the process, and even a snow leopard fails to catch a mountain goat. In one particularly relatable example, a student sits down to study only to get distracted by K-pop fancams. (We've all been there. Or at least I have.)

Naturally, the meme has found a particularly receptive audience among sports fans. Even NBA teams like the Orlando Magic and the Denver Nuggets have gotten in on the joke.

Think of it as the antithesis of a motivational edit. Instead of rewarding all that hard work with a triumphant moment of personal achievement, the meme celebrates the much more relatable experience of falling short.

You don't necessarily need to know who Jynxzi is to appreciate the joke, either. Much like other bits of streamer vernacular that have made their way into the wider internet lexicon (hey, chat), "almost almost" works just as well as a standalone reaction.

Sometimes, the grind simply doesn't pay off. But at least the memes do.

From YouTubers and TikTok stars to streamers and podcasters, Mashable talks to creators about how they built their platforms, the gear they swear by, and the trends they see coming next.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

Previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

She's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

#450. 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style, and he says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it’s been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I’m a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I’m above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn’t tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won’t be tolerated. But ‘it won’t be tolerated’ does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”

On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I’m going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results.”

“I also didn’t believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning; it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics: “There [were] also rumors that apparently I’m back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever plays a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”
