#402. Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany

Every three days in Germany, a man kills his wife or ex-partner. Every 10 minutes, the police record a sexual offense against a woman. "A shocking finding," according to Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig.

The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.

In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.

"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.

The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.

The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."

According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.

"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.

Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.

Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.

"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."

She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.

#401. Best Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth and Restoration (2026)

Hair loss isn’t always dramatic. It can be incremental. You start noticing a bit more scalp in harsh bathroom lighting, a tiny bald spot when you tie your hair up in a ponytail. The shower drain is more clogged than usual. Not long ago, hair-loss treatments meant topical remedies, supplements, or a flight to Turkey. Luckily, red-light therapy brings the potential for hair regrowth into your home—no clinical appointment required.

Beyond skin rejuvenation, clinical studies suggest red-light therapy can help energize hair follicles, increase blood circulation in the scalp, reduce inflammation, and lower dihydrotestosterone levels—a hormone that causes hair loss and thinning. Red-light therapy also supports adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, which helps provide oxygen and blood flow to the scalp and triggers follicles to remain in the hair growth phase.

To determine the best red-light therapy for hair growth, I tapped five WIRED tech reviewers who've dealt with hair loss themselves. We assessed red-light caps, hands-free helmets with full scalp coverage, and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation devices for 16 weeks. Along the way, I reviewed the research, spoke with dermatologists, and tracked ease of use. These are the favorites that produced meaningful results and earned our trust.

Be sure to check out our other wellness and skin-care guides, including the Best LED Masks, Best Hair Dryers, and Best Blow Dry Brushes.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Updated November 2026: I added the Capillus HairBand to Honorable Mentions, and I included a product to avoid. Prices, links, and product information were also updated.

To start, I consulted board-certified dermatologists and referred to clinical trials to help determine what features to look for when shopping for a device. I test these devices with several tech reviewers on our team, all of whom have personal experience with hair thinning or loss to different degrees. Most of these at-home gadgets call for a 16-week treatment cycle. We follow the brands' directions and record any visible results along the way.

We monitor changes in hair count, hair density, and scalp health, but effectiveness is only one of the factors we consider. We also judge ease of use, functionality, and comfort. We note the specific wavelengths of light and whether the treatment options feel tolerable or difficult to integrate into everyday routines.

We also prioritize safety, checking for FDA clearance, automatic shut-off features, and overall durability of the design. To date, our testers have not experienced any side effects, but we would have documented them had they.

I'm testing the Foreo Flip Play and the Theradome PRO Laser Hair Growth Helmet LH80.

CurrentBody's LED Hair Growth Helmet is a wearable, cord-free, Bluetooth-enabled device designed to improve hair density, thickness, and overall condition. After 12 weeks, I didn’t notice a difference in hair length—I did get a haircut halfway through testing—but I did spot new follicles sprouting along my scalp and sideburn area. My hairstylist mentioned that my hair felt thicker, and I noticed less breakage and hair caught in bristles when brushing. My balding roommate also tested the CurrentBody helmet, and he noted that his hair also felt thicker and that there was new growth around the scalp.

The circular earmuffs protect sensitive ears with a cushy, removable faux leather cloth, and they can be adjusted several inches up or down to ensure a comfortable fit. You can also connect the device to Bluetooth and play any type of audio during sessions, because God forbid I be left alone with my thoughts for 10 minutes a day. My only complaint is that the ear covers aren’t the easiest to adjust and would oftentimes pull out my hair when I removed the helmet. Nevertheless, this is the best red-light therapy for fuller hair. See my full review here. —Molly Higgins

At first glance, the HigherDose Red Light Hat looks like your everyday baseball cap, with a brand logo embroidered across the top—until you notice the little battery cap and controller on the back, or the 120 LED light bulbs lining the inside. While I don’t suffer from natural hair loss, I’ve struggled with trichotillomania since my teens. Part of what initiated the habit is that any time my sensitive scalp gets irritated, the itchiness drives me to pull at the hair around the spot. But in the months I’ve been using the HigherDose hat, I have felt like my scalp has been happier, with fewer irritated spots and overall itchiness, leaving me less likely to reach for my scalp. Last October, after my first month with this device, my hairstylist saw healthier regrowth instead of the breakage she usually sees. In January, she took another look and noted that my usual problem spot on the back of my head had grown in better than ever. She didn’t find any reaction on my scalp, either, from four months of using the device, and my roots look thicker all around my head.

Similar to my infrared brushes, I find that my hair is a tad oilier after use; both types of devices employ infrared light that can lock in moisture. It’s not a problem on days when my hair is clean, but if my hair is already dirty, using this hat requires an immediate shower. Overall, though, using the HigherDose hat has had a serious payoff for me, my scalp, and my hair. See my full review here. —Nena Farrell

I seem to rival a golden retriever in terms of shedding, and my sensitive scalp makes things itchy and flaky. To nip it in the bud, I tested the iRestore Elite device, along with the Max Growth kit. It sits right on the crown of your head, and it does heat up quite a bit as the red light puts focused emphasis on your scalp. The red-light exposure has helped prevent flare-ups, as I have none to note from my time testing it. That’s a feat in itself.

However, I’m not the success story here. I recruited a balding tester (my husband, who also gets to give products a spin) who wanted to give it a go to see if it would help with his receding hairline. After three months of consistent use, his hair density has bounced back significantly. It’s a regular sight to see him drink his morning coffee while waiting for the Elite’s 12-minute run time to wrap up. The accompanying Max Growth hair products smell wonderful, and they also played a contributing role in his follicular blossoming. Now, if only he would stop taking them out of my shower. See my full review here. —Julia Forbes

Unlike other devices on this list, GroWell is designed to be used every other day rather than every day to give your scalp a rest day to process the cellular stimulation (photobiomodulation). Also, unlike others, its wattage is limited to avoid oversaturating follicles past what studies show is the optimal 3 to 4 joules. What GroWell does do is treat your scalp with a proprietary combination of lasers and LEDs to create a blanket of energy you can feel lightly warming your scalp. (GrowWell's therapy-grade laser and LED diodes are proprietary to Apira, the company behind iGrow and GroWell, and are not the same as the generic diodes common in lower-end caps sold online.) The other big difference—which I would call a massive advantage—is separating those lasers from a bulky device. Instead, the GroWell is a flat pad that fits inside a baseball hat. There are hats included in the packaging, and I use them when I'm home. But this product is hassle-free to travel with (it takes up as much room as a pair of socks), and you can tuck it into any normal ball cap on a trip where you're flying carry-on only.

I've been using the laser cap for two months and have grown my always-thin and fine hair out for the first time in 15 years. It's worked well enough that I'm not asked as many questions about it as you might expect—everyone assumes I just shaved my head purely by choice now that they see me with a pretty regular amount of hair for a middle-aged guy. See my full rave here. —Martin Cizmar

Capillus HairBand for $600: Unlike this item's competitor, Hairmax's LaserBand, the Capillus HairBand is discreet enough that you can wear it in public. Unfortunately, in testing, it needed to be held in place most of the time. Editor Kat Merck also noted that the coverage area is naturally quite small and takes at least 15 minutes to run through her entire head. It's not FDA-cleared, but according to a Capillus rep, the company intends to have it cleared by 2027.

Laduora Duo 4-in-1 Red Light Therapy Scalp and Hair Care Device for $300: The Laduora Duo combines red-light therapy, microcurrent stimulation, sonic vibrations, and thermotherapy into one hairbrush-like device. I tested the device with the company's proprietary Boost Duo Pod ($30) serum for the first three weeks of testing, and it made my hair shinier and smoother. The metal bristles helped reduce buildup and revitalize the follicles on my scalp. Within about six weeks, I noticed baby hairs sprouting at the crown of my head and more fullness around my temples. See my full review here. —Molly Higgins

Hairmax LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex for $849: Unlike the usual helmet- or hat-based regrowth devices, the Hairmax LaserBand is a 3-inch-thick, flexible headband studded with 82 concentrated lasers rather than LEDs. (There’s also a slimmer, 41-laser version for $250 less.) Take it off its charging cradle and place it on one section of your head for 30 seconds, three times a week. When the time is up, it will buzz loudly; then you can move it to the next section. I appreciated the speedy treatment time, but the headband’s silicone teeth also didn't secure the band in place very well when I was treating my frontal hairline, so I had to stand still while holding it. However, it does work—after five months of testing, I saw definite improvement in growth along my hair part. —Kat Merck

Hooga Red Light Therapy Hat for Hair Growth for $299: I was excited to try this more affordable red-light hat after loving my experience with the HigherDose one, but I found myself unimpressed and actually uncomfortable while using it. The Hooga Red Light Therapy Hat looks like a baseball cap, but it doesn’t have a battery, so you have to stay plugged into the wall the entire time you use it. Feels a little pointless to look outdoor-ready when you can’t actually use it on the go. It also got too hot for me to wear comfortably. —Nena Farrell

Does Red-Light Therapy Work for Hair Loss?

Yes—research suggests low-level light therapy can work for certain types of hair loss, such as androgenetic alopecia, also known as male or female pattern hair loss. It can help increase hair count, thickness, and density by stimulating hair follicles and boosting cellular activity in the scalp.

That said, results depend heavily on the type and severity of hair loss. Red-light therapy works best in cases of mild to moderate thinning and may be less effective for advanced hair loss or scarring conditions like cicatricial alopecia. Consistency also matters. You typically need regular, ongoing use to maintain results, and benefits can diminish if treatments stop.

What Wavelength of Red Light Is Best for Hair Restoration?

According to the American Hair Loss Association, wavelengths in the range of 630 to 680 nanometers are ideal for hair regrowth. These wavelengths are known to support increased blood flow to the scalp, boost cellular activity, and help reduce inflammation. Some clinical studies specifically cite 650 nanometers as an especially effective wavelength.

Red-light devices that use medical-grade laser diodes tend to deliver more targeted and consistent light than standard LEDs, but both can stimulate hair follicles at the right wavelengths. For best results, look for FDA-cleared devices that list their wavelengths and power output.

How to Use Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth

Consistency is the most important part of any red-light therapy routine. Most devices require at least three months of use before noticeable results are observed, and some may take longer. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as treatment schedules vary by device, but most recommend sessions three to five times per week. The hair growth is preserved only with continued use, so you’ll need ongoing maintenance sessions.

Always start with a clean and dry scalp so the light can reach your hair follicles without interference from oils or styling products. Some devices include protective eyewear, and if yours does, wear it during treatment. Make sure to wipe the device down with a gentle disinfectant before or after each session to prevent buildup on the LEDs.

Topical regrowth treatments can complement red-light therapy and may help support thicker hair. A few randomized clinical trials suggest that combining minoxidil (2 percent or 5 percent) with red-light therapy can improve hair density and encourage faster regrowth compared to using either treatment alone. For a natural alternative, some research has found rosemary oil to produce results comparable to 2 percent minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia, though the evidence isn’t as extensive as it is for minoxidil.

If you’re pregnant or have an underlying medical condition, talk to your healthcare provider before starting any form of red-light therapy.

Is Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth Safe?

Yes—for most people, red-light therapy is considered a safe and noninvasive treatment with minimal side effects when used as intended. Still, it's always worth consulting a health care professional before starting any sort of treatment. This is especially the case for anyone with photosensitive conditions or autoimmune disorders that affect light sensitivity.

I prefer devices that are FDA-cleared because it means they've met certain safety standards for consumer use. But keep in mind that the clearance process is less rigorous than the FDA approval pathway, as it just requires manufacturers to prove their product is “substantially equivalent” to an already legally marketed device. Also, FDA clearance isn't a guarantee of results; it simply means it's considered safe to use as directed at home.

#398. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 26, 2026

The Moon is still looking almost full tonight, despite being a couple of days past the Full Moon. It's now in its Waning Gibbous phase, meaning the illuminated portion we can see is gradually getting smaller each night.

As of Thursday, Nov. 26, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Gibbous phase, with 96% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis, Kepler Crater, as well as the Tycho Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Gassendi Crater, the Endymion Crater, and the Posidonius Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 14 and 15 landing spots, plus the Descartes Highlands.

In North America, the next Full Moon will take place on December 23. In other time zones it will fall on December 24.

It takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a New Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#396. Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

"Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."

Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."

Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.

To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.

At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.

Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.

Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.

The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.

"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

#395. Hurdle hints and answers for November 26, 2024

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#394. The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The new Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

Most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.)

What's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, big-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

There's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

This Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

The Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

The milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re new to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

The Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so new espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

In the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.)

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

For those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

But this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This said, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

The Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

Sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

This streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

You can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is big enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

But note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

This Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a new college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk

The drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That said, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

This superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

But here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an issue on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

The delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

The guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell

The superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

Drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

De’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

The key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Setup and cleanup were especially important, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

Even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

Want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

If you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in big batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

Look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

Regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

First, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.

#393. China may not have planned Jensen Huangs affair with accused Chinese spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was returned to the job earlier this week, the board reinstating him amidst plummeting stock prices and apparent intervention from President Donald Trump. Now doubt is being cast on allegations that one of Huang's affair partners was a Chinese spy.

Huang has admitted to cheating on his wife with at least four partners as of this week, however his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) has drawn the most scrutiny. A former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, Ms. Huang is suspected of being an intelligent agent who shared information with the Chinese government and smuggled Nvidia chips into China, circumventing U.S. restrictions.

As such, Nvidia opened an independent investigation once Huang and Ms. Huang's relationship came to light, as well as established a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and export control compliance. Huang will also be interviewed by the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Select Committee on China, and House Intelligence Committee on Dec. 1, and testify before the U.S. Senate on Dec. 3.

However, the Wall Street Journal and New York Times now report that the U.S. has no evidence that the Chinese government directed Ms. Huang to begin an affair with Nvidia's CEO. Instead, current evidence indicates that the pair's extramarital entanglement may have been a matter of ordinary human infidelity rather than deliberate international espionage. U.S officials reportedly informed congressional staffers of this in a briefing on Nov. 24, the day after Nvidia reinstated Huang. This isn't to say that U.S. agencies didn't find any link between Ms. Huang and the Chinese government at all. U.S. officials reportedly stated that China's Ministry of State Security asked Ms. Huang to provide them with some unspecified information, which she allegedly did in accordance with Chinese law. They also claimed that her husband, businessman Kang Wei, was a Chinese intelligence asset. However, while the full extent of Ms. Huang's relationship with the Chinese government remains unclear, there is reportedly nothing to suggest that she passed on any significant information.

The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Ms. Huang was an intelligence agent. In an Oct. 30 press conference, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun called such reports "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." He later reiterated China's stance after Huang revealed his first affair on Nov. 8.

"On the so-called 'Chinese spy,' we have made our position clear," Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said in a Nov. 12 press briefing. "China's sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation. The U.S. should stop fabricating the 'Chinese spy' narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions."

The U.S. government currently restricts Nvidia's chip sales to China, citing national security concerns. Several other categories of foreign-made devices are also banned from entering the U.S. due to national security, including WiFi routers and robot vacuums.

#390. German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite

German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.

For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.

A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.

As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.

Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.

Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.

Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.

"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.

That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.

Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.

Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.

Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.

In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).

That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths" during the 80th anniversary of the 1945 agreement.

Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.

Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.

When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.

"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages."

Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.

In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.

Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.

Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.

The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate from the employee agreement, according to Haipeter.

Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.

Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.

"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union, said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work."

The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.

"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration."

Dudenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their jobs.

"We need a mediator along these lines," Dudenhöffer said.

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang to its top job earlier this week, the four-time adulterer pledging he'd be "a better CEO the second time around." Many supporters applauded his return, including prominent figures such as U.S. president Donald Trump, Tesla's Elon Musk, and OpenAI's Sam Altman.

All that said, no case is perfect, and the hinge is tricky to protect. Dbrand chose a two-piece design: The iPhone slots into the main back part, and the front has tiny tabs you remove to stick it to your iPhone Duo with adhesive. I’m not a fan of using adhesive; it’s easy to remove, though you obviously lose some stickiness (you get an extra set of stickers in the box). I worry that the front may get pushed off over time as the hinge slides over it, but so far so good.

Famous for its origami-style folding folios, cases, and wallets, Moft is a brand I like. The Dynamic Folio works great because it’s a simple cover that attaches magnetically. It extends beyond the Duo’s dimensions, with a solid camera surround to provide a little protection. The cover opens and folds to act as a stand or serve as a comfortable grip. The stand works with the iPhone Duo open or closed in landscape or portrait, and is surprisingly stable.

While I love the functionality, the Dynamic Folio looks a little dull. I’m not sure how much protection it would provide in a fall, though there’s also a full-case version that the back of your iPhone Duo slots into, but it costs an extra $20. As much as I like this, it feels overpriced for what it is. Constantly folding the cover out of the way can get annoying, and I’m not sure how well it will age.

Slim and very good-looking, this Mous case has a back panel made with Aramid synthetic fiber, with a matte black surround that provides a little grip. It’s a one-piece design with its own flexible hinge (no adhesive required), and it doesn’t add too much bulk to the iPhone Duo. The buttons and port are easily accessible, and there’s a raised lip around the camera module and cover screen. The minimal hinge cover doesn’t interfere with opening and closing the phone.

The big downside is that the Duo’s hinge isn’t fully protected. If you’re unlucky enough to drop it on the hinge, you could end up with a big repair bill. It’s also relatively pricey. Mous does have a version with a hinge cover for an extra $10, and it also comes in different finishes, including walnut wood, leather, and speckled fabric, but I haven’t tried it yet.

Maybe the simplicity of a big, chunky, one-piece case appeals. Smartish has you covered with the Gripzilla. This iPhone Duo case protects the phone from every angle, with heavily reinforced corners providing serious drop protection and an indented hinge cover that makes it very comfortable and secure to hold. The finish is pretty damn grippy, though it doesn’t quite match Dbrand’s case above. It is thicker, though, with lips around the cover screen and camera. I’m confident your iPhone Duo would survive a fall while wearing this, and it’s relatively affordable.

While it’s a one-piece case, the actual hinge is two very slim bits of plastic, and the hinge cover slides over the top when you open it and feels a bit janky. The button cutouts are quite deep, and it can be a little tricky to access Touch ID. I tested the plain black version, which is very dull, with nothing to distract from the ugly chunkiness, but you can get versions with a back panel featuring flower blossoms, mountains, or a contrasting green color.

If you prefer something a little slimmer and cheaper, I also quite liked the Smartish Gripmunk ($30), and it comes in various finishes.

I didn’t love every iPhone Duo case I tried.

Aulumu Aduo Particle Case for $90: Super slim, with an Aramid fiber case that the back of the Duo snaps into, this case minimizes bulk. The cutouts are good, and there’s protection around the camera. I also quite like the pattern, with dots of color on the back. The problem is that the front part of the case is a different material in a slightly different tone, and it relies on adhesive to stick to the front (mine kept coming loose). There’s also no protection for the hinge.

UAG Mouve XTE Case for $85: I usually like UAG’s stuff, but this is another two-piece case that relies on adhesive for the front part, so there’s no hinge protection. While there’s a lip for the camera and the cover screen, the sloping width leaves no room for a screen protector. The potentially handy fold-out ring on the back for secure holding and deployment as a stand feels like cheap plastic. Most two-piece cases like this are very slim, but this has UAG’s trademark angular chunkiness, just without the actual protection. It’s a rare misfire for the brand.

There’s a world of iPhone Duo accessories out there, but these are the ones I’d pick based on my limited testing so far. Many of the picks in our best MagSafe accessories and best MagSafe chargers guides will also work well with the Duo.

I’m impressed by this screen protector, considering it’s only $20 for a two-pack. The application tool makes life easy, and you get a cleaning kit to make sure your iPhone Duo is dust-free before you begin (take your time). I got a couple of air bubbles, but they were easy to push out. It is slightly smaller than the actual screen to accommodate most cases, but cases with a thick front bezel will buckle up or lift the screen protector. If you don’t plan to use a case, choose a different screen protector.

A stand is more important than usual for the iPhone Duo, and you ideally want something that can prop it up when it’s open, so you can take advantage of the large inner display. This ring works well, offering an adjustable angle no matter which way you prop the Duo and whether it’s open or closed. It feels sturdy, with two adjustable hinges, and the magnets are strong enough that you can also hold it by the ring with confidence. It’s just a shame it’s so expensive.

Your iPhone Duo can serve as a handy notebook or sketchpad. If you use the USB-C cable that came with your iPhone Duo to plug in an Apple Pencil (USB-C), you can pair it, enabling you to scribble notes, annotate, or sketch on the cover screen or the larger inner display. Sadly, it doesn’t support the Apple Pencil Pro or other models, so make sure you get the Apple Pencil (USB-C).

All the MagSafe wallets I’ve tried are designed for regular iPhones, so part of them extends beyond the bottom edge of the iPhone Duo. This one is no exception, but it still works well as a fold-out stand, looks stylish, and fits up to three cards. You can prop the Duo in landscape or portrait, and open or close it when you turn the wallet sideways. This is our top pick, but you can find some alternatives in our best MagSafe wallets guide.

Apple’s iPhone Duo supports wired charging at up to 60 watts and wireless charging at up to 25 watts, but you only get the top charging rates with the right gear. For wired charging, you need a charger that supports USB PD 3.2 with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) rated at 60W or higher and a capable USB-C cable. For wireless charging, you need a charger that supports Qi2 25W. Other chargers will still work; they’ll just be slower.

This updated version of our favorite MagSafe power bank supports Qi2 25W, enabling the maximum iPhone Duo wireless charging rate. It also packs 10,000 mAh of power, enough for a full charge with change, has a handy kickstand to prop the Duo up, and sports an LED display that shows remaining power and other stats. It will extend below the bottom edge of the Duo, since it’s designed for regular iPhones, but that’s true of the current crop of MagSafe power banks.

As the best of the best wireless chargers, this is what lives on my nightstand. It can wirelessly charge the iPhone Duo at the maximum 25-watt rate, and it’s heavy enough that you can remove your phone one-handed. You can also attach the open iPhone Duo in portrait orientation (in landscape, it tilts to one side). There’s even a spot around the back for your wireless earbuds to charge.

If you also have an Apple Watch and AirPods, you might prefer this charging tree that can juice up your trio of gadgets.

This wireless charging car mount works just fine with the closed iPhone Duo, keeping it topped off while you drive.

If you prefer wired charging at the maximum 60-watt rate, I recommend pairing this cable (or the cable that came with your iPhone Duo) with the Anker Nano Charger Neo ($26) or Apple’s 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max ($39).

#383. Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence

Germany's women's football team are to wear UN Women badges in games against Argentina and Peru, as domestic violence hits a record high in Germany.

Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.

UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.

Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.

"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic."

Germany captain Giulia Gwinn said in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this important issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence."

The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.

During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.

Ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.

Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.

Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the issue, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.

In sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal issue that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.

"Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action."

Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.

"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.

"The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures."

Sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.

They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.

"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.

"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.

"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert said. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so."

Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.

"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.

"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles."

Germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.

Support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.

After all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will."

This article was originally published on November 28, 2024, and updated on November 25, 2026.
